findings.evidence:

findings.recommendation: The proposal promises that the button "erases the member's personal data", but delete_account only stamps deleted_at and clears password_hash: the users row keeps email, display_name, phone and postal_address (app/schema.sql) indefinitely, with no retention rule, so a member who deletes their account still has every personal field stored (GDPR Art. 17 erasure, Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation). Since orders keep a user_id pointing at this row, the orders are not "without personal data" either. Overwrite or NULL the personal columns in the same UPDATE (email needs a unique non-identifying placeholder, e.g. 'deleted-<id>@invalid', and display_name a placeholder, since both are NOT NULL), keep only what accounting needs, and add a test asserting the row no longer holds email, display_name, phone or postal_address after delete_account. State how backups holding the old row are purged (retention period).
findings.title: Account deletion keeps the member's e-mail, name, phone and postal address

findings.recommendation: analytics_id is a deterministic salted hash of a small sequential integer: whoever holds ANALYTICS_SALT can recompute it for every user id, so analytics events keyed by it remain personal data (pseudonymous, not anonymous — GDPR Recital 26), and delete_account does nothing to the analytics data carrying it, so erasure misses that copy. The function is also unused in this change and not in the proposal. Either drop it from this change, or state where analytics events go (processor, EEA or not), their retention, and how a deletion reaches them (delete the member's events, or rotate to a per-user random id that is destroyed on deletion). Confidence low: the analytics pipeline that would consume this id is not visible in the repository.
findings.title: Analytics pseudonym survives deletion and is re-identifiable with the salt
